newsitem.title: CANADA: Chretien waits to see if he'll lead Canada again.
newsitem.headline: Chretien waits to see if he'll lead Canada again.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien, who almost lost the country in a referendum on Quebec independence in 1995, was awaiting Monday's Canadian election to find out if he would lose his majority government.
Chretien -- the self-styled "little guy from Shawinigan" (Quebec), due to his rough-hewn background -- is actually a millionaire who has long mingled with Canada's political and business elite.

A veteran of three decades in politics, he called the election 1-1/2 years before constitutionally necessary, to try to cash in on a big lead in the polls. But the campaign has raised the possibility of a reduced majority for his Liberals or even a minority government.
"Part of it is not surprising. When you have four candidates beating up on one candidate, it suggests that support for the Liberals will go down," said Reuters pollster John Zogby.

As the front-runner, Chretien was attacked by the leftist New Democratic Party for slashing government spending and by the right-wing Conservative and Reform parties for too much taxation and spending. The secessionist Bloc Quebecois said he did not do enough for Quebec.
"You have to be where the right says you're left and the left says you're right, so you're right," Chretien quipped in a campaign stop in Edmonton, Alberta, last week.

Chretien, described by his biographer as having a "chain-saw voice," enjoyed pumping hands during his campaign, urging supporters to choose a vision of a united Canada where government still had a role to play in careful spending.

"Our choice is to see the job through, to secure our future together, to finish the work of balancing the budget that we started, to secure programmes Canadians need and want," he said as he launched the election call at the end of April.
The Liberals have dominated Canadian politics this century, but Chretien has left himself open to criticism on the economic front and on how to deal with Quebec.
"You are better placed to decide how to spend your moeny than Jean Chretien in Ottawa," Conservative leader Jean Charest told a rally in Quebec.

Ironically, Chretien is more popular outside his native Quebec than inside the French-speaking province, where many federalists think he was too nonchalant in the tightly fought 1995 referendum campaign and where separatists believe he has betrayed the province.
"Chretien is the curse of Quebec," said Alain Robin, doing his groceries in the rural Quebec town of Montmagny. "Canada should stay together, but under Charest, not under Chretien."
The Reform Party ran a campaign ad saying it was time all Canadians had a say in keeping Canada united, not just Quebec politicians, drawing fire from Chretien.

But Chretien's Liberals have more support than any other party, due partly to a perceived lack of an alternative. They are especially strong in vote-rich Ontario, the prosperous central Canadian province that seems more content with the status quo than the others.
If the Liberals do perform badly in the election, commentators say, his days could well be numbered, with eloquent Finance Minister Paul Martin waiting to replace him.
"This tired Liberal champion needs soon to retire to pasture," the Toronto Star's Rosemary Speirs said on Sunday.
Chretien, 63, who mangles both English and his native French, has managed to cultivate his "aw-shucks background" in the same way Ronald Reagan did as U.S. president.

He refers often to how he came to Parliament in 1963 as a 29-year-old small-town lawyer who spoke little English, the 18th of 19 children born to a Roman Catholic family in a paper mill town in central Quebec.

Chretien is deaf in one ear and has a twisted mouth because of a birth defect -- which his Conservative opponents satirised in the 1993 election campaign, but which he unerringly turned around to make political hay.

Like Reagan, he is affable, often stumbling -- a Teflon man to whom few of his government's problems seemed to stick. Also like Reagan, he gives his Cabinet members great autonomy, even if it means he is often ignorant of day-to-day details.

Before becoming prime minister in 1993, Chretien held nine Cabinet posts under three prime ministers -- Lester Pearson, Pierre Trudeau and John Turner. In 1986, two years after losing the Liberal leadership race to Turner, he quit politics and returned to practicing law.
He was elected Liberal leader in 1990 and led his party to triumph with 177 of 295 seats in the 1993 election.
Chretien is married to his teenage sweetheart Aline, and they have a daughter and two sons.
